name: Probability of Success
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Where Do Those Probabilities Even Come From?
lesson.summary: Because expected value math is only as trustworthy as its probability inputs, this chapter looks at how the odds behind a moonshot bet like quantum computing actually get estimated, and why those odds deserve real scrutiny.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed how sensitive expected value is to a single probability estimate: moving the chance of a breakout outcome from 5 percent to 0.5 percent cut the expected ROI on a venture bet from 475 percent to 25 percent. So where does a number like "5 percent chance of breakout success" actually come from? Mostly from three imperfect sources: historical base rates from comparable technologies, expert elicitation surveys, and technology-readiness or S-curve analysis tracking how far a technology has progressed along its historical maturation path.

Base rates from comparable deep-tech sectors are sobering and worth anchoring against. In biotech, a drug entering Phase 1 clinical trials has historically had roughly a 10 percent overall chance of eventual approval, a commonly cited industry figure that varies considerably by therapeutic area. In early-stage venture capital generally, a large majority of startups, often cited around two-thirds or more, return less than the capital invested in them, with fund-level returns typically dominated by a small handful of outsized winners. Quantum computing does not yet have a multi-decade base rate the way pharmaceuticals do, its commercially oriented investment era is barely two decades old, so anyone quoting a precise success probability for quantum computing specifically is, at best, borrowing intuition from these adjacent fields rather than measuring quantum computing directly.

Expert elicitation, surveying physicists and engineers for subjective odds, tends to produce wide and poorly calibrated ranges for exactly the questions that matter most: when fault-tolerant quantum computing will arrive, and whether a given qubit modality will scale. This is not a knock on the experts. It reflects genuine, irreducible scientific uncertainty about problems, like scalable error correction, that have never been solved before, so there is no track record to calibrate against. A useful habit: when a probability for quantum success appears without any stated methodology, no named base rate, no named experts, no explicit model, treat it as a rhetorical number rather than an analytical one.

Technology S-curve analysis offers a rough outside view by comparing quantum computing's maturation against historical analogues. The transistor, invented in 1947, took roughly two decades to progress through integrated circuits to the first microprocessor in 1971. Classical computing's own path from room-sized 1940s machines to broad commercial viability spanned somewhere between two and four decades, depending on how commercial viability is defined. Quantum computing, dated from Shor's 1994 algorithm or from early physical qubit demonstrations in the 2000s, sits somewhere inside a comparably long maturation arc. That is not a probability, it is a pattern, but patterns are legitimate, if weak, evidence when nothing stronger is available.

The honest conclusion is unsatisfying but important: no one, including the physicists building these machines, can state a probability of quantum computing success with real precision, and every probability used elsewhere in this book's expected-value math should be read as a defensible order-of-magnitude guess, not a measurement. The right response is not paralysis, it is stress-testing: run the expected-value calculation at your best guess, then again at one-tenth and ten times that guess, and see whether the investment decision survives the range. If it only looks good at the optimistic end, you do not have an investment case, you have a hope.
